title: FCA explores quantum computing for fraud detection
excerpt: The UK regulator launches a quantum experimentation group to test machine learning applications in money laundering and fraud detection.
content:
Skip to content

9 Nov 2026

The initiative seeks to bridge the gap between emerging quantum capabilities and practical financial services applications, beginning with anti-money laundering and fraud detection.

The UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has launched the Quantum Experimentation Group (QEG), an initiative bringing together financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to explore practical applications of quantum computing in tackling financial crime. The group is established by a financial regulator and is scheduled to launch in the first quarter of 2027.

Initial experiments will focus on quantum machine learning for detecting money laundering and fraud. Participants will use an FCA synthetic dataset, based on artificially generated data, to test quantum-based approaches while addressing one of the practical barriers to experimentation: access to suitable financial data. The initiative aims to establish where quantum computing could offer advantages over conventional computing methods in addressing common financial services challenges.

Beyond technical experimentation, the QEG will help the FCA assess the technology’s potential, limitations and practical deployment barriers. The initiative will also generate insights into the challenges firms may face when adopting quantum computing, while strengthening industry expertise and encouraging collaboration between financial institutions, technology providers and researchers.

Financial services firms, quantum computing providers and national research laboratories can register their interest in participating by 31 December 2026. The programme will focus on early-stage experimentation and shared learning, with participation not constituting FCA approval or endorsement of any technology or solution.

Why does it matter?

Quantum computing could eventually change how financial institutions identify patterns of suspicious activity, particularly as financial crime becomes more sophisticated and data-intensive. The FCA’s initiative also highlights an important challenge for financial regulators: understanding emerging technologies before they become sufficiently mature for widespread commercial adoption. Early collaboration between regulators, researchers and industry could therefore help establish a more informed basis for future oversight, rather than leaving regulatory approaches to catch up with technological developments.
